**Why an AI agent forgets after a long session, and what a summary does about it**

**Scene 1: A friendly cartoon robot at a desk, sticky notes piling up around it as a chat scrolls past.**
Meet an AI agent. Give it a big job, and it works through a long conversation with you: reading, planning, trying things, fixing mistakes.

**Scene 2: The chat scroll keeps growing. A glowing window frame around the robot fills up and stops fitting new lines.**
But the model can only hold so much at once. Think of it as a window. Once the conversation grows too big for that window, something has to give.

**Scene 3: The long scroll is squeezed by a pair of hands into one short page labeled "Summary." The robot continues from that page.**
So the conversation is compressed into a summary. The agent then carries on its work from that short page, not from the whole story.

**Scene 4: Close-up of the summary page. A few sticky notes ride along; others drift off the edge and fade out.**
Here's the catch. Any detail that didn't make it into the summary is gone. Maybe a rule you mentioned early on, or a small decision made hours ago. The agent won't remember it, because to the agent, it never happened.

**Scene 5: A person holds up a quiz card in front of the robot; the robot answers, and checkmarks appear next to the old work.**
So how do we know a summary is good? We test it. We ask the agent questions about the old work. Can it say what was decided, and why? Can it recall what's still unfinished?

**Scene 6: Checkmarks turn into a solid, tidy page. The robot gives a thumbs up as the window clears.**
If the answers are right, the summary kept what mattered. If not, we improve it.

**Scene 7: Title card on a calm background.**
Long sessions don't mean perfect memory. They mean a good summary.
